sentence_chunk: Gender, Vulnerabilities, Livelihood and Heat  What does the fieldwork in Singarni talk about women, their livelihood, and vulnerabilities, and their relation with heat? Context Gender inequalities and gender roles play a significant role in the way different genders perform or function in a community. Their experiences differ in terms of their needs and preferences which usually varies along space and time. This affects the way in which they experience heat, and on a broader level, climate change. This study however, focuses to analyse ways in which women in Singareni cope with heat within their vulnerabilities and how they shape their daily life to adapt to increasing temperatures.

Our fieldwork in Singareni constitute 48 survey participants out of which 29 are women of various age groups, most of whom fall in the age groups between 25 and 45 years of age. Social Vulnerabilities Impacts of heat are not homogenous, even within smaller geographical areas. Along with the general vulnerabilities that are caused by extremities of the climate, there are social features as well. Social vulnerabilities include pre-existent internal conditions and norms that influence the positioning of a group or an individual during the impacts of a hazard. For instance, women are found to be using way less protection against heat while they are exposed to sun.

Anjali, a teacher at a private school, residing in government housing said once that they wouldn’t use umbrella or caps as a measure to protect them from heat as it would make them seem alien in the society. She said that umbrellas and caps are for people like me, who would come from different places, who are foreign to the community. Also, others in the community might mock them if they were to use them. She would prefer to use the ‘pallu’ of her saree or dupatta to cover her head when it becomes unbearable. Apart from this, women tend to sacrifice their comfort to help others in the family.

Sameena, mother of a two-year-old, said that she would only bath once to save water, whereas her husband and her mother-in-law who work outdoors would bath twice when the temperature rises. She would then shower during the evening after most of the house chores are done. She says, “or else I will start sweating again as I keep doing chores throughout the day.”Additionally, women also suffer from sleep deprivation as they often have to wake up earlier than the rest of the family, which adds to the discontinued sleep people experience during summers due to heat during night. Moreover, women, especially homemakers who spent most of their time in a day at homes, suffer from anxiety (“bechaini”) induced by sweat and fatigue during summers, as these settlements are ill- constructed with heat-trapping materials like tin and poor ventilation.

In addition to this frequent power cuts during summer add to the heat stress. A few of our female participants said that the reason for increased heat in their houses during summers were due to lower ceilings and less ventilation. Hence, most of them prefer sitting outdoor, under shaded spaces (trees or building shadows), or in their threshold spaces during the day when they are done with their routine chores.

Apart from these heat stress in women who suffer from certain female-predominant disorders like thyroid are also concerns to take into factor. Parvattamma who suffers from thyroid is a housemaid and her daughter said that her condition adds to her fatigue and sweating from heat. Another respondent Geeta, who has burns in her upper body also said that she suffered from increased sweating during her work. Shobha, another housemaid in her early fifties mentioned that she gets headaches while walking to and from work as she is exposed to sun during the time. Jaya, who cycles to and from her place of work said that she was once admitted to hospital due to heat stroke, she had a loss of appetite during the summers and that she compensated for having food by drinking more water.

Extensive exposure to sun along with malnutrition had deteriorated her health. She said that she would feel nauseating after work. Spatial politics Traditionally spaces outside houses especially public spaces were governed by men to gain access to resources. Women were more confined to private spaces and were more concerned with resources that were considered for collective use. This distinction between spaces that are free to occupy by different genders had developed a sense of hierarchy in the society which defined the value and recognition given to them.

This politics of gender, although in its initial phase of fading, is still prevalent in most places. As mentioned earlier, women and others, who stay home for a bigger proportion of their time in a day, to escape heat trapped in their houses, would sometimes prefer to sit outside their houses. This option of sitting outside is again governed by a lot of factors such as shade in a space near their houses where they would feel safe, such as their personal threshold space which extends a little after the boundaries of their house. More examples of such spaces include a familiar known house’s threshold space, the space between two adjacent houses which has shade casted by these two built forms, a common space like temple (like the one near Shobha’s place). Apart from safety, other factors that allow/restrict them from using these spaces include their caste/religion wherein certain spaces are dominantly used only by people belonging to a particular community, or that their husband would not like them to mingle with others outside the house.

They might use these spaces to perform productive work, or as a space of socialisation where they might sit and braid each other’s hair or just talk, or just help each other do a particular chore like drying chillies or segregating onions from the sack or to simply just go and sit idle or sleep.

Figure 1: A makeshift arrangement for paid work.  Most families in Singareni chose to send their girl children to residential schools. When asked about the reasons for this decision, safety and security emerged as the primary concerns. This preference for hostels stemmed from an incident of child molestation that occurred in Singareni in 2021, which made women particularly cautious about the safety of their girl children in the area. Anjali shared her perspective, expressing that Singareni was not a safe place for children, and she preferred her two girls and one boy to stay in the residential school until either she or her husband returned from work.

This way, she felt assured of their safety. During one of her surveys, once Sameena expressed her worry about Saniya, her 7 years old stepdaughter, who had gone to play with her two brothers. Sameena was concerned about the safety of the area and the potential risks that Saniya might face while playing there. Other respondents like Kumari and Nirmala had also sent their girl children to residential schools. Livelihood As mentioned earlier in this article, women in Singareni actively participate in paid work, and there is a diverse range of occupations they are involved in.

These include domestic services, ginger/garlic/onion peeling, street vending, tailoring, and various entrepreneurial ventures like bangle making, teaching, laboratory technician jobs, and housekeeping in public/private institutions such as hospitals. Additionally, some homemakers and others engaged in seasonal work turn to ginger/garlic/onion peeling as a secondary source of income. This activity has become one of the most accessible ways for women in Singareni to earn money. (I guess due to its availability throughout the year) Jayamma, a 50-year-old street vendor, began peeling garlic when her health deteriorated due to low blood pressure and other reasons, leading to limited employment opportunities. To make a living, she would sit inside her house, watching television while peeling garlic.

She mentioned that when it got too hot indoors, she would keep her door open and continue peeling garlic while sitting near the doorway. Figure 2: Two women who were sitting and chatting in one of their threshold spaces.

Geeta, a women in her late forties, a victim of domestic violence also does garlic peeling, and is her primary source of income. She spends most of her time in Road no 13 (see figure1) peeling garlic with 4-5 other women who come to do the same. Geeta who has burns all over her upper body had been advised by her doctor to refrain from this activity as they generate more heat and hence causes infection in her body. However, when questioned about why she persists in this line of work, she replied, "At the end of the day, I need to earn a living for my family. My husband doesn't contribute to expenses; whatever he earns, he spends on alcohol and gambling.

I have no other choice but to do this." Aiswarya, a teenager who housekeeps in DWC said that she has taken garlic which will earn her 400 rupees to save up for her brother’s birthday cake. She said the cake will cost her around 180 rupees, and when asked what she’s to do with the rest, she said she will save it for herself. (read more in Livelihood, Opportunities, Heat and Health.docx) Some women do engage in construction work. Their work is non-stable.

Nirmala a resident in road no 12 said that the contractor would tell them either a week prior or just the day before that they have work. They are paid daily wages. Further, important questions to think about-  ● How stable is the income of women in Singareni during the summer season? • Do women in Singareni need to seek additional sources of income during the summers? • If they do, what are some common jobs they take up?

• Do women in Singareni have the agency to explore other sources of earning if they lose their primary income? • Does the increase in unpaid caregiving responsibilities, such as taking care of children during summer vacation or attending to the sick due to heat-related issues, result in a reduction of the number of hours they dedicate to paid work?

Housing construction as a social process: Diverse building modalities, shaping diverse experiences of heat among the residents of Singareni Basti  19th July Arpita  Context Several plots in Singareni are physically transforming where residents are building, re-building or renovating their houses. At least 5 sites can currently be spotted which are under construction. There are more sites, where building construction got over recently. For many of them, the push to construct a new house has come because of the construction of new concrete roads in the Basti, with a height up to at least one foot above the original ground level. Hence, the floor levels of all the existent houses, have automatically gone down to a minimum of one foot below the road level.

Apart from everyday functionality issues such as the door levels below ground line, disappearance of protective thresholds at the entrances, dust in the house, etc.,the residents have faced or are concerned about facing severe consequences of flooding during monsoons. This situation has led to the renters vacating the low- floored houses and moving elsewhere. Moreover, the perceived owners are selling their properties to new people who often start construction with filling up the floor level with debris from the previous houses. Some residents are re-building their houses on their own plots.

Every new building now has a much higher floor level than the roads. However, for some residents the push to build a new house comes from a dilapidated condition of their previous housing, the need to vacate the old house due to contested ownership status, among other reasons.  Heat and housing The temperature sensor data from March to May 2023 collected from the kuchchaa and semi-pucca houses in Singareni already tells us about the level of heat exposure and heat-led vulnerabilities that prevail in that area. Physical character of houses, especially choice of building materials, level of ventilation, adequate space availability, building orientation, among other factors shapes residents experience of heat within their houses. Such decisions are taken either prior to or throughout the process of every new construction.

In case of Bastis, such choices and decisions are embedded within various social and economic complexities. The end-product or the building, at the end of the construction process then becomes a result of such complex relationships.

This study aims to explore the following questions: 1. What kinds of factors inform the materiality, construction process and spatial design of housing in present day Singareni? 2. Who are the major stakeholders and decision-makers (within and outside the households) who take such decisions? 3.

How do different housing (design and construction) arrangements shape people’s experience of heat in Singareni?  Firstly, the study aims to highlight that the process of constructing a house including the decisions around materiality, building techniques and design vary across households and are directed by specific socio-economic factors such as ‘sense of security or agency’, ‘financial capacity’ and ‘access to knowledge of building construction’. Secondly, it aims to understand how such decisions and choices create specific kinds of built forms with varying degrees of adaptive capacities to withstand heat.   Tenure insecurity  On asking the residents of Singareni (who are currently building or have built their houses) about the decisions or rationales around housing construction, it became evident that how confident they feel about investing in their house upgradation comes from how secure they feel in their current house and land. Among all the residents of the Basti who do not have a patta, different houses feel different about their security.

A respondent who thinks, having an RCC roof can provide them better cooling and additionally provide them a terrace space where they can sleep during hot summer nights, do not dare to build it due to the fear of eviction. The hesitation to build an RCC roof due to tenure insecurity despite having financial capacity is a phenomenon dominant across the Basti. However, these groups are planning to or currently have comparatively more robust houses with fly ash or ACC brick walls (several of them are plastered), more than one rooms, asbestos walls and fenestrations. Residents The above argument is a pattern that has emerged from the data of various open-ended conversations with the residents of Singareni, However, it needs to be further validated with baseline surveys, censor data, targeted interviews and FGDs with masons, construction workers, and residents who have recently built or are currently building their houses. Agency/sense of security, financial capacity, and knowledge of construction by shaping the construction processes, materiality, and physical design of housing  Informs Peoples’ experience of heat in the informal settlements of Singareni

who work closely with the gully, area or Basti leader or has strong connections with them, feel more secured than the late settlers or the residents without any such connections. This reflects in the way they are planning for their future houses.  Lack of financial capacity Another set of choices come from clear lack of financial capacity, who are building their houses out of an urgency without having been able to gather enough resources or finances for construction. Something particularly striking about one specific household of 4 members is that their new house is getting built with materials, and techniques poorer in strength and in resilience in terms of adapting to extreme weather conditions (there might be more such households). The family is currently moving from their existing kuchchaa house with fly-ash bricks and a tarpolin on bamboo-structured roof to their adjacent plot where they will build a house with asbestos walls and a tarpolin roof, without any window openings.

The new built form is possibly going to give them comparatively worse heat experiences, the next summer. On asking, if they have thought about how hot the house will get with such materials, the man of the house (a street vendor) said, they are doing the best possible, and he would sleep on his bandi (cart) if it gets too hot. Additionally, they would build this house (they call it a jhopdi) themselves with whatever little knowledge they have about construction, even though they know it will take them a month to complete the construction as they are incapable pf paying the mason charges (Rs 1200/ day in Singareni).

Key decision-makers and stakeholders Masons are the experts who take key decisions around materials, building techniques and design (including positioning and sizes of doors, windows and ventilators) while adhering to the budget of their clients. Within households, men of the house take major decisions around budget, finance and even space configuration. The masons and the teams of construction workers who work in Singareni are also the residents of Singareni. That way, physicality of built forms in Singareni is influenced by the knowledge, skills and expertise the masons and the construction worker community bring into the processes of construction. There are two specific cases of construction, where one house (completed) is built by the man of the house and his team, who is a mason himself, and the other house is built for the daughter of a construction worker who supported the mason in constructing her daughter’s house.

In such cases where the residents are the experts themselves, have more agency not just in terms of taking decisions for building the house, but also in terms of accessing affordable and improved building materials. Similarly, it is yet to be found, what happens when some residents have close relationships with these communities of masons?Does it impact, the total expenditure and the physical quality of housing?As a starkly contrasting example, the family who are building the Jhopdi for themselves on their own, lie within the worst range of precarity, where they do not feel secured enough about the land they are building on, do not have the financial capacity to build a semi-pucca house, have no access to any kind of skills and expertise (that of masons), no knowledge of building materials and of ways to procure them.

Housing construction as a social process The complex assemblages of social and economic factors are resulting into diverse typologies of built forms with varying levels of heat resilience in present day Singareni. Security of tenure directs residents’ willingness and non-willingness to invest in better climate adaptive houses despite their capacities. Repositories of knowledge present with the mason communities, directs the choices of materials, design, and techniques of construction. Relationships between house owners, masons and construction workers directs masons’ personal motivation, relaxation in labour charges (is a hunch so far), procurement of the most suitable materials and hence the end-result. Lack of financial capacity, lack of access of knowledge of construction and absence of personal connection with building communities together lead to the most precarious ways of housebuilding and to substandard housing quality.

The centrally planned Heat Adaptation Plans (HAPs), or even the state-run cool roof policies exclude the spectrum of vulnerabilities and the socio-economic complexities in the construction processes in low-income households. It is crucial to see housing construction beyond the scientific and technocratic lens and rather identify housing construction as a social process, especially in low-income informal settlements. It is crucial to identify the strengths and gaps in knowledge repositories that exist within the networks of local masons and construction workers in Bastis, who are also the key decision-makers. Strengthening these communities with knowledge of affordable heat-adaptive construction techniques and materials, equipping Basti residents with basic understanding of building construction, and material market can create internal capacities as well as healthy networks between diverse actors who can act as key stakeholders in the process of housing construction.

Land Tenure and Vulnerability to heat What does the fieldwork in Singareni tell us about the relationship between land tenure and vulnerability to heat?  Introduction Fieldwork in Singareni directs us towards a key insight, suggesting social Infrastructure like housing and built form plays a vital role in building resilience of households against periods of extreme heat waves. However, lack of legal ownership of land rights, commonly known as ‘patta’ deters them from building permanent structures that are heat resilient. This is largely due to the potential fear of evictions and their precarity of stay in a particular location. This significantly impedes their ability to prepare or cope with rising temperatures.

Context Our fieldwork suggests that only a handful of houses in Singareni hold ‘pattas’. These houses stand out prominently from the other informal structures in the neighborhood. The patta- holding houses are pucca, concretely built with defined boundary walls. In contrast, the informal houses are semi-pucca, non-engineered, temporary self-built housing without any defined boundary. These houses tend to extend spatially as occupants seize any opportunity to occupy adjacent plots of land whenever possible.

These informal houses were initially recognised as ‘jhopris’. The precarity of their living in the settlement was clearly evident from temporary structures being built out of bamboo, thatched roof, tarpaulin sheets or coconut leaves. Most of these houses have been built on encroached lands that were available for free for poor migrants to come and occupy during the early 2000s. Later, two consecutive fire massacres in 2003 and then in 2008 caused a significant shift in the materiality of housing from bamboo and thatched roof structures to asbestos sheet houses, the next cheapest alternative. While the transition was a temporary solution to their exposure to the recurrent fire hazards in the neighborhood, the fire resistant attribute of the asbestos sheet has significantly increased the indoor temperature of the houses.

With poor thermal and insulation properties that trap heat inside the house, this materiality shift has made the residents more vulnerable to heat stress. Disrupted sleeping patterns, inability to get rest affecting their productivity and unbearable working and living conditions inside the house have been some of the common responses from the residents during the summers. According to them, thatched roof houses were cooler compared to the

tin sheet houses. On the other hand, the land tenure situation in the site still remained unchanged.  Tenurial Insecurity and Infrastructural Exclusion Absence of ‘patta’, largely excludes the settlement from formal planning processes by governments. Lack of legitimacy as formal housing, disconnects them from formal grid arrangements. Consequently, they face persistent challenges in securing access to infrastructures such as water and electricity.

With only a limited number of households actually being able to afford sophisticated cooling technologies, tenuous access to key infrastructures like water and electricity make life in the neighborhood a constant struggle with rising temperatures. The residents merely make a living out of patched and makeshift arrangements by deploying a wide range of tactics and politics.  While patta-holding houses have piped water connections to their houses, the non-patta houses lack piped water connections. Instead, water is predominantly supplied by informal arrangements such as water tankers provided by Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (HMWS&SB). The tankers are the primary source of water supply that frequent the neighborhood every alternate day.

However, our respondents mentioned that relying solely on tanker water is insufficient to meet the household water consumption needs, especially for houses with larger family sizes. As a result, they configure their access to other informal water arrangements using social networks, political affiliations and other traditional makeshift strategies. Accounts of our respondents reveal that the water supply arrangements in the neighborhood are multifaceted and very complex. Hence, the absence of patta largely affects a household’s access to water, which remains one of the critical infrastructures to beat the heat during summers.

Source: Author. This tap that projects out from a concrete walled house shows people relying on other sources of water supply in the neighborhood other than the water tankers. The tap has a direct connection to an overhead water tank (OHT) placed on the roof of the house. The water is pumped to the OHT using motors and pipes. This water in the tank is kept as a stock, which is used whenever they fall short of water.

Similarly, the lack of legitimacy deprives them of metered electricity connections. Their electricity is either hooked from the main pole or is hooked from other household’s hooked connections which results in incidences of short circuits and voltage fluctuations. This is evident from the chaotic electricity networks that characterize the neighborhood. This results in frequent damage of electrical appliances owned by the households. The voltage fluctuations also restrict their ability to use cooling appliances as per their preference.

Residents residing in asbestos roof houses make do with fans operating at very low speeds even in intense summers. One of our respondents also narrates the difficulty of getting an electrician to get the appliances or the pole repaired in an informal settlement. He mentioned that the electrician usually is either unwilling to come or he needs to be paid more to get things repaired.

The picture shows a tangled network of electrical wires that is extended from the electrical poles to the individual houses  The neighborhood's lack of legal recognition prevents authorities from enforcing waste collection and disposal schedules. Moreover, the absence of tenure security in the neighborhood leads to a lack of ownership and responsibility among residents, resulting in careless waste disposal practices. Consequently, dumping grounds have formed within the neighborhood, posing hazards and located in close proximity to government quarters. The foul odor emanating from these dumping grounds makes it impossible for residents in government housing to open windows or doors for ventilation during summers.

As a result, living conditions inside the houses become extremely unfavorable. These instances provide overwhelming evidence of deprivation within the settlement, caused by absence of tenurial security.  Perceived tenure security and limited agency in informal settlements: Implications for Heat Resilience   Among the informal structures, while some have been occupied through squatting, others have been rented. In either case, they lack the agency to make any adjustments to the house that helps them cope with the heat. Lack of willingness to invest in the house is evident from gaps and openings in the roofs of the houses exposing the residents inside the house to high temperatures and harsh rains.
They are poorly planned without proper orientation and ventilation that largely results in heating up of the house. Majority of respondents revealed

that their willingness to invest in a house depended on their perceived tenure security i.e the duration of their stay in a particular location. Households residing in the neighborhood for 20 years or more express their intention of building their houses bit by bit.  Conversations with respondents also indicated that their willingness to invest in the house also depended on the political control they exerted over the area and if they were financially more sound than others. One of our respondents, who is a real estate agent, says he is one of the most prominent leaders in his alley. He was among the first few settlers who captured a couple of land parcels in the area.

He has been living in Singareni for 25 years and says that, when he first shifted here, he lived in a tarpaulin hut. But over the decades, he started feeling safe and wanted to invest in the house bit by bit. (“Before my youngest son gets married, I will complete building my house”). His renovation plan includes removing the old broken tin roof into either a slab (if he has money) or tin, and replacing the portions with asbestos walls with brick (AAC) walls. He would need 5 lakhs rupees to complete the renovation.

Their socio-economic condition of the residents further discourages them from making any long term investments on the house. In more than one instance, we have uncovered that the residents have either taken loans or are seeking a loan to refurbish the house. The respondents conveyed that the renovation became necessary as it was increasingly difficult for them to endure the rain and heat. We have also come across statements that reveal that even if some residents possess the financial capacity to purchase and install air conditioning units or coolers in their houses, they refrain from doing so due to a range of reasons. First, they admit that the walls of the houses aren't feasible to drill and install the AC units.

Second, the area has consistent voltage fluctuations on the account of the electricity being non- metered. The fluctuations damage the electrical appliances and hence, repairs of these appliances are pretty common during summers. One of our respondent during an interview stated,  “Recently, my fan has stopped functioning. I have given it for repairs. I usually take them for repair to Shailabad chaurasta, near Dhobighat.

The fan repair is costing me Rs.300. The burning of appliances mostly happens during the summers.” Fieldwork in Singareni also directs us towards another key insight, that indicates that residents perceive legal water and electricity connections, along with meters, as crucial prerequisites for acquiring the allocation of 'Patta' or legal land rights. Accounts of one of our male respondents states his ongoing struggle to obtain legal ownership of their lands through land title deeds or ‘pattas’ for more than a decade.

“We are fighting for a meter. Once there is a meter, there will be water supply; once there is water supply, we might be given a Patta.”  In this context, the meters associated with these connections serve as tangible evidence of their right to exist and occupy the land. Other respondents also reaffirmed this perception and revealed that they would prefer a metered electricity connection even if that would entail an increase in his household expenses.

Livelihood, Opportunities, Heat, and Health  Out of a wide range of work that is done by the residents of Singareni, some are spatially located within the Basti. The nature of work ranges from being home-based work such as bangle making, recycled plastic bag making, garland making, copper-wire extraction, etc.to being jobs that happen in shared community spaces or commercial nodes such as waste segregation and selling. Jobs like cleaning, sorting and peeling garlic and ginger takes place both inside and in threshold spaces of individual houses, as well as in common commercial spaces where a group of women does the same job in a common area. Each of these jobs involve direct contact with various materials which becomes a prime aspect of their experience of work.

While assessing exposure to and effect of heat on Basti dwellers involved in diverse livelihoods, the materiality of work emerged as an important theme. It became crucial to understand how a worker feels while handling a certain kind of material during the summer months. While every kind of local work have their own set of opportunities and challenges, it was interesting to see how some specific set of work because of the materials they involve have harsher heat effects on the people doing it.  From the responses of multiple people who work with ginger and predominately garlic, it has become evident that when they handle kilos of ginger and garlic either within their homes or at the depot, their hands feel the heat from the material themselves. They experience this especially in the summers.

They often use the word, “ungli/haath tadakta hai”, meaning ‘fingers and hands burn’. Damaged thumbnails, fine cracks on fingers and palms, heat rashes are some of the conditions that is seen on the hands of these women who peel and sort ginger and garlic regularly. Hands of just women because this job is highly gendered. The men associated with these materials are either arranging the stock at the depot or are selling the stock on their carts.  Unlike the women who peel/sort ginger-garlic under some kind of shade, families and individuals mostly belonging to the ‘Lambada’ community in Singareni can be seen sorting sacks of dry, wet scrap directly under the Sun during peak heat hours.

The predominant material they deal with are plastic, glass, and cardboard, though the scrap is often mixed with food and other organic waste. They carry a few bottles of water with them on to the ground where they do this work. They do this job within a time range of 5 am till 1pm. The ending hours often cross 40 degrees in May. It is still to be investigated what do they specifically experience while dealing with the materials, but the practice without a proper local facility is only possible in a large open area that is difficult to be shaded through makeshift

arrangements. A woman who was doing this work along with her three sons, was upset that she cannot eat anything till midday until she completes the sorting work out of the disgust, she feels while handling garbage and only survives on water. This makes her work the most difficult during the summers.  While all these work types involve a lot of exposure to heat in different ways, there responses on asking them their most favourable weather to work, are surprising. On asking a woman who sells and peels garlic at the depot about her most preferable season to do her work, she said, “summers” because she gets maximum orders for ginger and garlic during summers.

On probing further about in which season does she think, her body would be most comfortable doing that job, she paused... thought a bit and said, “maybe when it rains”. A woman who makes bangles using chemicals to decorate the bangle frames with glitters in a very congested space in her house, says she feels the hottest while cooking and while making bangles. Additionally, she often looks worried, when her toddler approaches her amidst work due to the fear that the child might touch the chemicals. On being asked if she is relieved now because it is monsoon already and the weather is cool, she refused. She said, she prefers summers because, the chemicals do not stiffen up and remain fluid-like, that helps her make more bangles in less time.

A family that sorts and sells scrap said that summer is the best season for them to work, because the garbage remains dry and much more convenient to handle in the summers than in the wet season.  The study will explore the dichotomy that exists between how the body of these workers respond to heat while handling specific materials and their desperation to grab maximum economic opportunities in the most thriving business season.

Ginger-garlic peeling: a job that provides safety net to the women of Singareni  Ginger-garlic peeling and sorting is more than just a category of livelihood in Singareni. For the women of Singareni, it is that anchor that they can rely on during their times of financial difficulties. It is also something that young girls can take up to take care of small special expenses that is outside their monthly budget.  The business runs primarily from two three locations in Singareni (yet to investigate about who are the business-owners), where ginger and garlic is either given to the basti women for sorting and peeling for Rs 50/ kg or is given to the street vendors to sell and take portion of the profit. The word ‘given’ and not ‘sold’ is used, because even the street vendors do not pay for procuring bulk stock for selling.

The business runs through network of trust and faith, where women get work and earning any moment, they need it. The timings are flexible and the process of procuring the material is not complex or cumbersome.  A woman (40 years old) who is a street vendor has not been vending from the past few months because of her sickness and her broken cart. To manage the daily expenses these days, she goes and gets a few kgs of garlic and peels them for a living. A young girl (12-14 years old) has got 8 kgs of garlic to peel, so that with this earning, she could buy a birthday cake for her brother.

"What does the fieldwork in Singareni tell us about the relationship between building materials, architecture and vulnerability to heat?"   Building materials in Singareni colony reflect, primarily, the amount of capital that a family is able to invest in their home. Broadly, there are 5 kinds of materials used, in varying configurations. Concrete is uncommon, but not unseen. It is mainly used for creating the walls of homes.

Using concrete as roofing is completely unseen, even in otherwise pucca houses. This is likely due to the significant increase in cost and complexity that comes along with it. Importantly, more than one person mentioned that they were not “allowed” to use concrete for roofing. One person mentioned that it was because the local leader – Saddam – would not allow it. Another said that it is because they don’t have patta for their houses.

Importantly, concrete is also the material used in the Government Housing buildings. Much of this concrete has begun to degrade, with steel rebars now sometimes visible because of years of weathering. Concrete – especially in the GH buildings – tends to be relatively better at insulating the houses from the worst of the heat. In some of the houses we visited, keeping the windows and balcony door closed kept the house at a much lower temperature compared to the houses in the informal settlement.  Fly-ash or ACC bricks are the most common type of pucca housing material.

It forms the bulk of the pucca houses walls and interiors. If a house has solid walls, it is likely that it will be using this kind of brick. It can either be used bare or with a covering layer. This usually includes a layer of plaster which may be painted - and even textured, perhaps by using the ends of reed brooms to scrape across the plaster before it dries. Many of the newer houses feature this kind of finish on their façade.

It is unclear what the thermal properties of these bricks are, but they are certainly better at insulation than asbestos/metal sheeting. However, since these houses still have roofs made of sheeting, and relatively few or small windows, they are often very uncomfortable.

Asbestos sheeting and metal sheeting (“patra”) are both commonly used, both for roofing and for walls. In the case of roofs, they are the choice for the most pucca of houses. Here, they are inset into the frame of the walls of the building. [x picture]. It is not always clear when these sheets are asbestos or metal.

In less pucca housing, sheets may be used as walls, usually in combination with other kachha materials. These are almost always asbestos, since it is far stiffer than metal sheets. In the first image, see painted asbestos being used as walls, besides a decidedly pucca house made of AAC bricks. This house, too, has a sheet roof. In the second image, see the sheeting embedded in the walls to form the roof.

These materials are particularly common in kachha houses, and as the roofing in semi-pucca houses. It is likely that the metal sheeting are the worst at insulation, given most metals are extremely conductive. Asbestos has traditionally been understood to be good at insulation, which should suggest that it makes living spaces more comfortable. However, the makeshift construction of the kachha houses likely prevents any serious insulation.

Tarpaulin is commonly used in the informal settlement, either by itself or in combination with another material. Because it is cheap and waterproof, it is used as roofs or walls in the most insecure housing. It may often be weighed down by stones or other heavy items to prevent it from flying. It will be important to see if there is a transformation in the colony regarding the use of tarpaulin now that the monsoons have properly set in.   Tarpaulin offers very little protection from heat, except for its provision of shade, which is certainly better than nothing.

Near Geeta’s shop is made of bamboo and tarpaulin, and while it does not feel any cooler than ambient temperature, it certainly (subjectively) helps to create a shaded space outside the direct sunlight.  Wooden poles and bamboos are used as structural members in kachha houses. They may be used to prop up asbestos/metal sheeting, or to drape/hang tarpaulin over.    Architecture styles and priorities in the settlement vary. The least secure housing usually consists of a combination of tarpaulin, sheeting, and bamboos or wooden poles.

These houses are relatively uncommon, but not absent. More common are houses built of AAC bricks, with a roof made of sheeting. The sheet may be secured to the top or inset into the frame of the house. Some of these houses will have painted exterior walls, often with a textured finish. The specific style and comfort of these houses can vary greatly.

Many of the newer houses are built at an elevation from the road. The recent concretisation of many of the internal streets raised the level of the road to the extent that many houses were now nearly a foot below the road-level. These houses are now at significant risk of flooding. There are many

houses built this way in the settlement. Most of the newer houses are built at a height, to prevent the risk of flooding. This is discussed in more detail in Arpita’s essay on recent housing.   Houses will usually have one or two windows, along with several ventilation panels near the roof. Most houses have fans, though few have exhaust fans.

The small and cramped space, as well as the minimal ventilation, can make certain activities particularly uncomfortable. In particular, many women mentioned cooking as the most uncomfortable activity that they have to do at home – multiple women said they have to step away from the stove and stand outside the house for a few minutes every so often because of how hot they feel while cooking. Sweeping is another activity that causes a lot of discomfort, as it requires switching the fan off. The role of masons and local builders is explored in more detail in Arpita’s essay, where she discusses the costs and considerations of hiring a mason, as well as the role they play in the design of houses.  In the government housing colony, houses usually follow a similar layout.

All houses have balconies, which are in line with the façade of the building. However, there has been a great deal of improvisation and modification of these houses. Especially at the ground floor, many people have extended or enclosed this space in order to increase their house area. There are also a number of flats where the street-level balcony has been converted to a kind of shop. In some of the upper floors, too, there are extensions jutting out of the building.

In the GH colony, many of the narrower streets are filled with garbage. One explanation offered by the residents is that the people living on the upper floors tend to throw the garbage out of their windows. As the stench of the garbage does not reach all the way up, it is the people at the bottom floors who have to face the consequences. 1      Feeble Water Infrastructures and Thermal Comfort in Singareni    One way to understand Singareni colony’s water politics and vulnerability to heat is through understanding the water histories in the area. During my fieldwork in Singareni colony, I could not help but wonder: how is one supposed to take measures against heat when they do not have proper infrastructure for water and electricity?A simple, seemingly obvious question felt so important to ask and answer. In the often-had conversation of ever-increasing emissions due to increasing air conditioning, where does a place that does not have water and electricity connections fall?Here, there is no space to lament about the paradox of air conditioning.

This place falls outside this question, as it does outside the “grid”.  Most residents of Singareni Colony are off the grid; they do not have any piped water connections, nor do they have metered electricity connections. What they have in terms of water access are about ten borewells and HMWS&SB (Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board) tanker supply on alternate days. The water tanker supplies 1.5 drums (250 litres capacity) for each household, regardless of the household size. The residents of government housing, although have piped connections and metered connections.

A few years ago, the street on which Jangaiah – a resident of Singareni Colony – stays did not have even a borewell. They had to manage with the one and a half drums of water they got from GHMC water tanker, once in two days. Kamalamma, from the same street, told me that they used to take a bath once in two days – even in the summers – for the lack of water. They could not even think of using an air cooler in such a situation. Things changed a little in their favour when in 2020, they were able to get the I. S. Sadan Division Corporator, Sama Sunder Reddy build and inaugurate a borewell, right before the GHMC elections.

This is one of the ways in which residents in Singareni Colony use their citizenship to gain access to some infrastructures. The Singareni Banjara Vinayaka Committee, a committee of ST people from Nalgonda district, successfully negotiated for a borewell to be built for their street by using their citizenship in a unique way. A national coordinator of All India Adivasi Congress – a wing of Indian National Congress – from their village in Nalgonda, where they have voting rights, agreed to build a borewell for them back here in Singareni Colony. Some others pooled money to get a borewell built for their neighbourhood.  This is some – although not enough – improvement from where they started out.

Decades back, the residents of Singareni, many of whom settled there 20 years ago, used to walk two kilometres to the Saroornagar lake to bathe, due to the lack of hydraulic infrastructure. In the words of Leela, a resident:   "This was water that people like you wouldn't even stick your feet in. We used to bathe in it. [The water] was much worse back then. Buffaloes used to bathe in the lake, and we, right next to them.
We have always had to walk for water, even now we have to walk to carry water from our drums that the GHMC water tankers fill. Our legs are vehicles that do not have brakes."

2     During that time period, the residents of Singareni colony had to travel to RTC Nagar or Karmanghat, located two kilometres away, just to buy water for the day’s needs.  However, things are still tough for people like Parvatamma, who does not have a borewell near her house, and has to rely on tanker supply for the most part. On days that the tanker fails to supply water, she is forced to get water from a Masjid in Singareni Colony, which has borewell water. She is not allowed to take water from the “ST borewell” located right next to her street. Although, that is not the case with all borewells.

Some borewells, according to other residents, are opened to people from other streets when the tanker fails to come.  This points us to the reality of heat adaptation in Singareni Colony. Even simple adaptations to heat – especially water- and energy- reliant adaptations – are not easy to use here. As simple as the mechanism of wetting the floors for thermal comfort is, it relies on water. The lack of water infrastructure effects their ability to use the easiest mechanisms for heat relief.

In the words of Parvatamma,   “Even if I wet the floor with water, it evaporates in seconds. What is the point?There is not enough water to keep wetting the floor enough for it make a difference. So, we do not bother with it. I have diabetes, hypertension and thyroid disease.

These [summer] days, I am terrified of any work (pani ante bhayam aithundhi); it causes a lot of sweating and exhaustion. I try to rest whenever I can. What used to take me half an hour to do, now [in the heat of summer] takes me one hour. I also have to go to work and am left with very little time.”  It is also one of the reasons that Parvatamma’s household uses the air cooler sparingly; only her son uses it and during afternoon hours when the heat is at its peak.

There is not enough water for the cooler to be used for everyone in the house. Fetching water itself is physical exertion, and a chore carried out by women and girls.  Another respondent spoke about the effects of hard water from the borewell on the functioning of the air cooler/motor; the deposits from hard water put the motor in dysfunction over time (Tanaya’s field notes). In Singareni Colony, I found that the air coolers fall into frequent disrepair and need regular repair and maintenance. Some residents have to go through two or more repair cycles in the same summer.

There are many reasons for that. One pertains to the very make of the coolers. Air coolers require some level of maintenance; more so if the coolers are second-hand. Other reasons related to electricity voltage fluctuations, hard water, and lack of water, among many others.   For example, the last summer, Rekha, a resident of Government Housing apartments, had issues with water.

Even though the residents there have household taps and are on the grid, there were issues with the water not coming regularly. For lack of water, they used a new air cooler without filling water in it, which ended up damaging the motor of the air cooler. Rekha says that they were completely aware that it would cause damage.  “What else can we do?There was no water.

So, we used it as a pedestal fan because we really needed it in the summer. After the motor got damaged, we sold the cooler.”  Even though Rekha stays in Government Housing and has household taps, there is still a problem relating to water; besides the fact that the water comes every alternative day, it only

3    comes for about one hour and fills only two drums. Outside of this, it is very tough for them to acquire water in any other way as they live on the third floor and cannot carry the water all the way up.  Residents of Singareni Colony rely, to an extent, on water sources from schools, masjids, and madrasas. In summer, some residents use the water pipe from a government school in the government housing area to wet and cool the common area outside it. According to Niranjan, a Government Housing resident, it gives them some relief when they escape the heat in their homes in the afternoons.

This space serves as a spot for leisure and rest.  The madrasas and masjids of Singareni Colony play a role in providing some water and some legitimacy to some in the colony. Through political patronage of the MLA of the constituency, who is from the AIMIM party, local leaders like Saddam and Khader get madrasas and masjids built. The masjids, in turn, serve as a visible political symbol that give some legitimacy to demands placed via them. As Khader, a “local leader” puts it:   “We were able to raise demands for municipal taps to be provided for every street in Singareni Colony.

For a while, the municipal taps were sanctioned by HMWS&SB and used to run from 11am to 4pm every day. However, there was uproar caused by the contamination of the pipes. Some of the ST residents dug up the pipes to illegally connect it to their houses. The water around it, stagnant and full of disease, entered the pipes. After that, a small boy died from consuming contaminated water.

The Water Board decided to want none of these headaches. They removed the municipal taps… We were also able to raise demands for tanker supply through the masjid.”  The masjid’s water taps are open for all and is used as a buffer when there is no water, especially in the summers.  Conclusion   To sum up, a lot of factors inform Singareni Colony’s vulnerability to heat, including water infrastructures (and the lack thereof), electricity, building materials, and built form, among others. One can see people trying to find shaded areas to sit at, when their indoors become too unbearable.

One can see kids play with the water that escapes the tanker pipe when the drums are getting filled, and people rejoice in the temporary coolness that the tanker water spillage brings. But, beyond that, if some relief has to be felt, a lot of labour has to be put in: if one has need to feel the cool of the air cooler, they must put in the labour of walking to the borewell in the scorching sun, filling a pot with water, carrying it back and filling the air cooler. It is worse if the household has a high head count, as they would need that much more water to satisfy needs.  The people of Singareni colony have made multiple arrangements to try and fill in the void pertaining to water infrastructure. Still, in the words of Leela, “[the people of Singareni colony] are vehicles that do not brake.”
Any meaningful level of thermal comfort in Singareni colony is only possible if it gets placed on the grid and gains water connections.
